prompt.context: Your client is a multinational pharmaceutical and biologics company. The client has a portfolio of drugs for major disease areas, including cancer, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal diseases, to name a few. The client has experienced a decline in revenue over the last 18 months, and is fearful of further declines, especially given that its most commercially successful drug, which treats acid reflux disease, will be going off of patent in May of next year.
prompt.question: What are the areas they should look into to change the course of this trend?

clarifying_info.q: Can you tell me more about the revenue breakdown by product or disease area?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, here is Exhibit 1 showing company revenues by disease area.

clarifying_info.q: Is the revenue decline concentrated in any particular geography?
clarifying_info.a: Over two-thirds of the Purple Pill's revenue comes from the US.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current pricing and margin structure for the Purple Pill?
clarifying_info.a: Current revenue per pill is $1 at an 80% margin; total revenue from Purple Pill is approximately $3.2B.

exhibits.title: Company Revenues by Disease Area (in $B)
exhibits.shows: A table listing four drug categories with their drug name, disease area, percentage of 2013 revenues, percentage change in revenues, and market share trend.

framework: Identify this as a revenue problem driven by product mix and patent risk
Analyze revenue by disease area / product (Exhibit 1) to isolate largest declining segments
Assess industry trends: generic entry, pricing pressure, regulatory changes, geographic mix
Evaluate competitive dynamics: market share shifts, new entrants
Size the patent cliff impact on the Purple Pill specifically
Develop strategic options to preserve Purple Pill revenue post-patent expiry

questions.prompt: What are the largest drivers of revenue decline over the last year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should review Exhibit 1 and note: overall business is declining ~10%; Neuroscience (Green Pill) is the biggest percentage decliner at -40%; Cardiovascular (Red Pill) is also declining at -8%; Respiratory (Blue Pill) is growing at +10%. Candidate should then calculate dollar losses per drug to identify the largest dollar contributor to the decline.

math.setup: Total 2013 revenues = $21B. Use % of 2013 revenues to find current revenue, then back-calculate prior year revenue using (1 + % change), and compute the dollar loss.
steps: Red Pill: 22% x $21B = $4.6B current; prior year = $4.6B / 0.92 = $5.0B; loss = $5.0B - $4.6B = $0.4B ($400M)
Purple Pill: 15% x $21B = $3.15B current; prior year = $3.15B / 0.98 = $3.21B; loss = $3.21B - $3.15B = $0.06B ($60M)
Green Pill: 7% x $21B = $1.47B current; prior year = $1.47B / 0.60 = $2.45B; loss = $2.45B - $1.47B = ~$1B
math.answer: Green Pill is the largest dollar driver of decline at approximately $1B lost, followed by Red Pill at ~$400M.

questions.prompt: What issues could have caused the Green Pill's decline?
questions.guidance: Acceptable answers include: lower price, lower tablet sales volume, generic competition entering the market, regulatory restrictions, out-of-stocks, currency and geographic trends. Strong candidates will connect generic entry to any market share loss visible in Exhibit 1. Interviewer confirms: the decline is attributed to introduction of generics in the US and other established markets (50% of decline); remaining declines relate to Medicaid liability and inventory issues.

questions.prompt: Given the Green Pill experience, evaluate the three options to maintain as much revenue as possible from the Purple Pill when it goes off patent next year. The options are: (1) Do nothing, (2) License the brand to an OTC manufacturer for $250M one-time revenue, (3) Direct-to-patient campaign online with 3rd-party delivery. Assumptions: without action Purple Pill loses 20% of annual volume (as with Green Pill); current revenue per pill is $1 at 80% margin, total revenue ~$3.2B; OTC license: 10% of current volume transfers to OTC brand (we get only one-time $250M); Direct-to-patient: retains 25% of the 20% that would be lost, but margin drops to 50%.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute gross profit for each scenario and compare. Beyond the math, a strong candidate discusses short-term vs long-term implications: licensing looks near-breakeven in year 1 but provides no additional revenue in year 2; direct-to-patient is incremental but risks cannibalizing higher-margin business if not priced correctly.

math.setup: Base: total Purple Pill revenue = $3.2B, current margin = 80%. After patent expiry, 20% of volume is lost without intervention.
steps: Do nothing: retained revenue = $3.2B x 80% = $2.56B; gross profit = $2.56B x 80% margin = $2.05B (casebook rounds to $2.0B)

License OTC for $250M: start from Do-Nothing gross profit $2.0B; add $250M license fee; subtract cannibalization from 10% volume transfer at 80% margin: 10% x $3.2B x 80% = $0.256B; net = $2.0B + $0.25B - $0.256B = ~$2.0B (roughly breakeven vs do-nothing in year 1; no $250M in year 2)

Direct-to-patient: start from Do-Nothing gross profit $2.0B; add retained volume benefit: 20% lost x 25% retained x $3.2B revenue x 50% margin = 0.20 x 0.25 x $3.2B x 0.50 = $0.08B; total = $2.0B + $0.08B = $2.08B
math.answer: Do nothing: ~$2.0B gross profit. OTC license: ~$2.0B in year 1 (breakeven), less in year 2. Direct-to-patient: ~$2.08B gross profit, incrementally better than do-nothing.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some issues that could have caused the Green Pill's revenue decline?

categories.name: Generic / competitive entry
ideas: Generic manufacturers entering after patent expiry
Market share loss to lower-cost alternatives

categories.name: Geographic and macro
ideas: Shift in prescribing patterns by region

recommendation: The direct-to-patient program is the preferred option in the near term: it retains ~$2.08B gross profit vs ~$2.0B for do-nothing, and preserves the brand without giving away margin permanently
OTC licensing is economically near-neutral in year 1 but is a long-term loss since the $250M is a one-time payment and the cannibalization of existing high-margin volume is ongoing
Do-nothing is the floor; acceptable only if implementation costs of the other options outweigh their modest upside
risks: Direct-to-patient program could cannibalize existing 80%-margin prescription volume if patients shift channels rather than representing net-new retention — must price the DTC channel to prevent margin dilution
OTC licensing brand halo risk: a low-quality OTC product could damage the prescription brand's equity
Geographic concentration: over two-thirds of Purple Pill revenue is in the US, so US generic entry will have an outsized impact regardless of strategy chosen
next_steps: Model year-2 and year-3 economics for OTC licensing (no $250M recurrence) vs DTC to confirm DTC advantage over a 3-year horizon
Assess incremental cost to build direct-to-patient fulfillment capability; if cost exceeds ~$80M NPV, reconsider
Explore pricing strategy for the DTC channel to protect margin; consider whether a premium OTC price point could compensate for the margin reduction
Evaluate geographic sequencing: prioritize US retention strategies given concentration of revenue
